title: What Did I Ask You to Do, by When, and for Whom?: Passion and Compassion in Request Management
research_question: How do knowledge workers manage person-to-person requests across organizational contexts and communication channels, and what implications do those practices have for request-management system design?
methodology: The accessible source provides only the paper abstract, which characterizes the work as an exploratory examination of diverse work practices and representations used for person-to-person requests in organizations. It discusses recurring problems including requests being distributed across communication channels, aggregation and prioritization difficulty, contextual variation, and the social character of request management. The abstract does not disclose participant counts, recruitment, data-collection procedures, or the detailed analysis method, so those aspects cannot be verified from the available source.

key_findings.finding: Request management combines personal task management with collaborative-work concerns because requests carry both interpersonal relationships and organizational accountability.
Person-to-person requests are scattered across multiple communication channels, making them difficult for workers to aggregate into a coherent view.
Prioritizing requests is difficult and request-management practices differ according to work context.
Knowledge workers can expend substantial effort managing requests while also taking account of the burden and efforts of their colleagues.
The authors propose treating requests as socially implicated work objects and derive design implications for services intended to support request management.

limitations: Only the abstract was accessible, so the empirical sample, data-collection method, analysis procedure, and scope of the underlying study could not be verified.
The accessible abstract reports no quantitative evaluation, agreement statistics, or benchmark comparison.
The accessible source does not establish longitudinal tracking of explicit work-item states such as new, open, resolved, or superseded.
No reproducibility artifacts or public dataset are identifiable from the accessible source.
raw_claims: Managing requests is simultaneously a collaborative-work problem and a personal task-management problem.
Organizational requests are distributed across multiple communication channels.
Workers have difficulty aggregating requests into one manageable representation.
Determining which requests deserve priority is difficult.
Request-management practices vary with organizational and interpersonal context.
Workers may invest unusually large amounts of effort in keeping track of requests.
Request management is socially embedded rather than merely an individual to-do-list activity.
The authors argue that system design should account for the social relationships surrounding requests.
